title: Fungal Infections in People Living with HIV and Other Immunocompromised Patients: A European and Romanian Narrative Review
content: Background. Fungal infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality across the growing population of immunocompromised patients, although the underlying immune deficit differs between people living with HIV/AIDS, non-HIV hosts (hematologic malignancy, neutropenia, solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation), and critically ill patients rendered transiently immunosuppressed by severe illness itself, as during the COVID-19 pandemic. Objectives. To compare epidemiology, pathogens, diagnosis, treatment, resistance, and prophylaxis across HIV, non-HIV immunocompromised hosts, and COVID-19-associated fungal disease, and to examine, as a regional case study, how this picture is represented in the European literature and in Romania specifically. Methods. Narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE literature on HIV and non-HIV immunocompromising conditions, including COVID-19 associated conditions, complemented by a targeted search for European cohort data and by pathogen-specific PubMed searches for Romanian primary literature. Diagnostic terminology follows the EORTC/MSGERC consensus definitions, complemented by the ECMM/ISHAM criteria for COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA). Results. CD4+ depletion in HIV produces a predictable, threshold-driven pattern of opportunistic mycoses; non-HIV immunosuppression is more heterogeneous; and critical illness — as exemplified by COVID-19 — introduced a distinct risk state, with COVID-19 Associated Pulmonary Aspergillosis (CAPA) incidence ranging from ~1% to >20% in ICU patients across European cohorts, and COVID-19-associated mucormycosis (CAM) reaching epidemic proportions in India. European cohorts otherwise document a one-year invasive fungal disease incidence of ~10% after allogeneic HSCT, up to 17% in acute leukemia, and 3–14% for aspergillosis after lung transplantation. Romanian evidence consists of single-center mycological studies, three Candidozyma (Candida) auris reports (including a genomic study assigning all sequenced isolates to clade I), case reports and small series of aspergillosis, CAPA and mucormycosis (the latter increasing after COVID-19), a nosocomial fusariosis outbreak in an acute leukemia ward, one cryptococcal-meningitis series, environmental detection of azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus, and a modelled national burden estimate; no dedicated series exist in solid organ transplant recipients or patients with solid tumors. Conclusions. Recognizing these divergent, population- and context-specific patterns is essential to risk-stratified screening and treatment; the Romanian case illustrates how national surveillance can lag far behind recognized burden even within a well-characterized global framework.
